chunks: 3. Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Imran al-Daqqaq (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Muhammad ibn Abi 'Abd Allah al-Kufi narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Barmaki, who said: Al-Fadl ibn Sulayman al-Kufi narrated from al-Husayn ibn al-Khalid, who said: I heard al-Rida, Ali ibn Musa (peace be upon them), saying:

Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, has always been All-Knowing, All-Powerful, Ever-Living, Ever-Lasting, All-Hearing, and All-Seeing. I asked him, 'O son of the Messenger of Allah, there is a group that says: Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, has always been All-Knowing with knowledge, All-Powerful with power, Ever-Living with life, Ever-Lasting with antiquity, All-Hearing with hearing, and All-Seeing with sight.' He (peace be upon him) replied, 'Whoever says this and accepts it has taken other gods with Allah, and they are not under our guardianship at all.' He then added, 'Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, has always been All-Knowing, All-Powerful, Ever-Living, Ever-Lasting, All-Hearing, and All-Seeing by His Essence. Exalted is He, the Elevated, the Great, from what the polytheists and anthropomorphists say.'

key_terms.الْمُشَبِّهُونَ: Anthropomorphists (those who liken Allah to creation)
key_terms.عُلُوًّا كَبِيرًا: Exalted with a great elevation (Quranic phrase for divine transcendence)
key_terms.قَدِيمٌ: Ever-Lasting / Ancient (one of the divine attributes)
key_terms.لِدَاتِهِ: By His Essence (indicating identity of attribute and essence)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between Allah's attributes being 'with' His essence versus being His essence in Shia theology?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies the nature of Allah's eternal attributes by refuting the view that attributes like Knowledge and Power are distinct entities separate from His Essence, a position he links to polytheism (tawassuf). He affirms that these attributes are identical to His Essence (Dhat), thereby upholding the Shia doctrine of Tawhid al-Sifat while remaining exalted above the descriptions of both anthropomorphists (Mushabbihun) and those who distinguish attributes from essence. This hadith serves as a key reference in the debate between the Akhbari and Usuli schools regarding the nature of divine attributes.
